analysis.one_liner: Rewrites the Clean Air Act's toxic air pollution program to force sharp cuts in hazardous emissions and require hazard assessments at chemical facilities.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill passed its Senate subcommittee in October 1989 but never got a vote in the full Senate committee or on the floor, and died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul how the EPA controls hazardous air pollutants. It would list toxic chemicals for regulation, set strict emission limits for major industrial sources based on the best reductions achievable, forbid cost from weakening standards meant to protect people from cancer, and require permits, monitoring, and leak detection at polluting facilities. It would also require chemical plants to assess and disclose the risks of catastrophic accidental releases, create a federal Chemical Safety Board to investigate such accidents, and launch a program to monitor and cut toxic air pollution in big cities.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near or downwind of industrial facilities—especially residents of large cities, where monitoring and an urban air toxics program target pollution from many small sources—would gain from sharp cuts in cancer-causing and toxic emissions. Communities near chemical plants would gain from mandatory hazard assessments and a new independent board investigating accidental releases. Workers and neighbors would also gain from leak detection and monitoring requirements.", "who_benefits_short": "Urban residents near polluting facilities

how_it_helps.text: It replaces the old Clean Air Act program, which had regulated only a handful of toxic chemicals in nearly two decades, with a system that lists an initial set of hazardous air pollutants, adds more on a five-year review cycle, and lets any person petition to add or remove a substance.

It requires emissions standards for major sources—those emitting 10 or more metric tons a year of a listed pollutant or 25 tons of a combination—set at the maximum reduction achievable, with a congressional benchmark of 90 percent reductions from uncontrolled levels for existing sources.

For carcinogens, it sets a floor on allowable lifetime cancer risk for the most exposed person, with strict standards that cannot be weakened by cost considerations, and mandates further tightening if residual risk stays above one-in-one-million for the most exposed individual.

It creates a Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board to investigate catastrophic chemical releases and requires facilities to prepare, update, and make publicly available hazard assessments covering worst-case accidental releases of extremely hazardous substances like chlorine, ammonia, and phosgene.

It requires air monitoring in metropolitan areas over 250,000 people and directs EPA to build a national strategy for reducing urban air toxics from small 'area' sources, which hit dense neighborhoods hardest.

analysis.who_pays: Industrial facilities that emit hazardous air pollutants—chemical plants, refineries, and similar major sources—would bear the cost of emissions controls, monitoring, leak detection, permits, and fees. Some of those costs would likely be passed to consumers in prices. Small 'area source' emitters in cities would face lighter but real requirements.", "who_pays_short": "Industrial polluting facilities

drawbacks.text: The bill's health-based standards bar EPA from weighing cost, cost-effectiveness, energy, or technological feasibility in setting the strictest standards, which could impose very expensive controls on some industrial sources.

Facilities handling listed substances would face new obligations—hazard assessments of worst-case release scenarios, updated every two years, plus monitoring, leak detection, and reporting—adding paperwork and compliance costs.
The bill requires expanded federal and state permitting, monitoring in large metropolitan areas, and a new investigative board, which means ongoing public spending and administrative burden.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits—fewer cancer-causing chemicals in neighborhood air and fewer catastrophic chemical accidents—would have been substantial for people living near industrial facilities, which is most of the urban population. The costs fall on a specific, identifiable industry in the form of control equipment, monitoring, permitting fees, and disclosure of hazard assessments, and the bill does contain real flexibility: a voluntary 90 percent reduction exemption, hardship extensions, and de minimis waivers. The honest counterargument is that rigid no-cost-consideration standards can drive expensive controls at high cost per unit of health benefit, and those costs can be passed on in prices. On the whole the bill's design was a serious, detailed attempt to fix a regulatory program that had covered only a handful of chemicals in nearly two decades.

outcome.mechanism: The bill got a favorable subcommittee vote but never cleared the full Senate committee, never reached the Senate floor, and was never taken up by the House before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Senator Durenberger introduced S. 816 on April 18, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.
The Subcommittee on Environmental Protection held hearings on September 21, 1989.
On October 19, 1989, the subcommittee approved the bill favorably with amendments for consideration by the full committee.
No further action is recorded: the full committee never voted, the Senate never voted, and the House never considered the bill before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industrial emitters of toxic air pollutants, which avoided the new emissions standards, permits, hazard assessments, and the Chemical Safety Board that the bill would have imposed.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start: 10 Senate Democrats and 3 Senate Republicans cosigned, and the bill never became a partisan fight because it never left committee.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturing and industrial emitters of toxic air pollutants
industries.note: The bill would force the industry to install maximum-achievable emissions controls (with a 90 percent reduction benchmark), obtain operating permits, monitor leaks, and publicly disclose hazard assessments of worst-case accidents. It would also face a new federal board investigating its accidents. Its cost of compliance is the public's gain in reduced exposure.

A specific provision directs EPA to assess hydrogen sulfide emissions from oil and natural gas extraction and implement a control strategy, subjecting the industry to new emissions controls. It also faces the general source standards like other emitters.

industries.industry: Small industrial and commercial facilities in urban areas
industries.note: Even 'area sources' too small to count as major sources would face monitoring-driven state programs and control strategies, though the bill directs EPA to provide generic, low-cost compliance tools for small facilities.
